summary:
Crew Health is a personal health monitoring app for astronauts on long-duration missions, built with Python and Streamlit. Each crew member signs up, sets a preflight baseline, and records heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, exercise, and mood. The records are stored locally to reflect an onboard, offline setting.

It addresses the challenge by turning health indicators into clear, actionable guidance. Readings are compared with each astronaut’s own baseline and color-coded at a glance. A body view flags areas needing follow-up, trend charts reveal gradual change, guided measuring helps non-experts, and next steps explain when to contact flight surgeons. Environment context covers spacecraft, stations, rovers, and moon bases, while a points-for-logging routine encourages consistent check-ins.

It matters because on Moon and Mars missions, communication delays make crews responsible for catching radiation-, isolation-, and gravity-related health changes early. Crew Health supports that self-care while keeping mission medical protocols in charge. It is decision support, not diagnosis, and its thresholds are illustrative pending validation with NASA data.
details:
Crew Health: project details

What it does and how it works

Crew Health is a personal health dashboard for astronauts on long-duration missions.

Sign up and baseline. Each crew member creates an account, enters their mission day, and sets preflight baseline values (heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep).

Log readings. They record heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature, sleep, exercise, and mood in a few taps. Short how-to-measure guidance supports people who aren’t medical experts.

Assess. Each reading is compared with that astronaut’s own baseline and labelled Near baseline, Below or Above baseline, or No data. Color coding makes the status clear at a glance.

Act. A body view flags what needs follow-up (sleep and mood, cardiovascular, bone and immune health). Trend charts show gradual drift, and next-step cards explain when to follow protocols or escalate to flight surgeons. Context lines change for a spacecraft, space station, rover, or moon base.

Stay consistent. A daily mission routine awards points for logging, not for “good” readings, with streaks and a check-in.

All records are stored in a local SQLite database, so the data stays on the machine.

Benefits

  • Early warning from slow changes (such as declining sleep) that one-off readings can miss.
  • Personal baselines instead of one-size-fits-all thresholds.
  • Plain-language guidance for non-experts.
  • Works without a connection, which suits communication delays on Moon and Mars missions.
  • Private by default, with a CSV export the crew chooses to share.

Intended impact

To help crews catch radiation-, isolation-, and gravity-related health changes earlier, so small problems don’t become critical ones. It supports astronaut self-care and gives flight surgeons better information, without replacing mission medical protocols. It is decision support, not a diagnosis.

Tools and technology

  • Language: Python (plus HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG for the animated body view)
  • Libraries: Streamlit (interface), pandas (data handling), matplotlib (charts)
  • Storage and security: SQLite, with salted PBKDF2 password hashing from Python’s standard library
  • Hardware: none beyond a standard laptop. The tool is designed to take manual entries now, with sensors and wearables as a future input.

What is creative about it

  • A body view with status call-outs and subtle, clearly-labelled-illustrative motion (a breathing outline, and a pulsing dot at the latest heart rate).
  • A points-for-logging routine that rewards honest tracking, so astronauts have no reason to hide or “game” bad readings.
  • Environment-aware context for four mission settings.
  • A condensed single-screen overview that makes health status quick to read.

Factors we considered

  • Communication delay and offline use: local-first storage and clear escalation guidance.
  • Users who aren’t medical experts: guided measuring and plain language.
  • Safety and honesty: the app states it is not a diagnosis, and it never claims certainty.
  • Privacy: data stays onboard unless the astronaut shares it.
  • Accessibility: keyboard-friendly controls, and animation turns off for users who prefer reduced motion.
  • Limitations: the thresholds are illustrative and need validating against NASA Human Research Program data. The login is demo-grade, not production security. Readings are entered manually for now.

Next steps: radiation-exposure tracking (using the CSA resource), wearable and sensor input, a flight-surgeon view, and testing with crew feedback.
